chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
title: Lois Deppe and Wylie Avenue on the Hill
summary: Early memories of Lois Deppe, and going to Wylie Avenue to hear music before turning professional.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: He may have. The early recollection I have of Lois Deppe is by way of those Gennett records that he made and of course then after, as I say, when Harry came back he formed his own little combination, The Red Hot Peppers which was a 4-piece group and for a while he had a show on local radio station that came on about 4 o'clock in the afternoon and I sang -- I appeared on his show a couple of times while he was on the air. I imagine he must have had a show for about a year.

And then just about this time I was old enough to sort of go downtown where the music was and tag along behind Harry and get into some of the clubs and hear music, and especially up on Wylie Avenue at the Crawford Grill. This is where most of the musicians would hang out.

Is in Pittsburgh, downtown -- well, Pittsburgh, up on the hill they called it.
And that's the, I suppose what you could call the strip kind of, it's the place where all the night spots were located, musicians hang out?
Yes. Well, Wylie Avenue I'd say was about ten or twelve blocks up from downtown Pittsburgh where all the stores were, so most of the clubs were out there.
On the interview with Lewis McMillan you describe it as up on the hill, I think.

Well, it is on a hill. Before I got my first so-called professional job at the Benjamin Harrison Literary Club, I went up on the hill after I got through doing a little gig out in East Liberty, because I had this audition for the Benjamin Harrison Literary Club which was downtown. The Banjamin Harrison Literary Club was an after-hours spot. I think in the early days it must have been a

speak-easy. But this was at the beginning of the repeal, so it was considered legitimate, although it was a hangover from the speak-easy days.

I went up on the hill to listen to some music and also to find out from some of the musicians directions to get down to 966 Liberty Avenue, and that was the night of the flood, the big flood that they had in Pittsburgh. And that's how we got to realize just what an advantage the hill was. The water was coming up so fast -- that was one of the worst floods that they've ever had, you know, in Pennsylvania. As a matter of fact it's second to the Johnstown Flood which was earlier in 18-- something, I don't know, the big Johnstown Flood.
